feedback: If a learner expects nothing to change when trees are removed: point out that with fewer leaves transpiring, there is less vapour, so the clouds shrink and the rain falls off — the loop is weakened.

If a learner says all the rain blows in from the sea: agree that some moisture does come from the sea, then show that the leaves themselves also release vapour that rises and condenses here, so the forest recycles much of its own water.
Reinforce the term: 'The water leaving the leaves as vapour is called transpiration.'
When the learner restores trees and the rain returns, confirm: 'The forest makes much of its own rain — the trees are part of the pump.'
activities.intendedInsight: The rainforest is not just receiving rain — the trees release water vapour through their leaves (transpiration), which helps form clouds and rain over the forest, so removing trees weakens the rain. This is a feedback loop, not only a one-way supply from the sea.
learnerActions: Watch a forest cross-section where water climbs the trunks from the roots, puffs out of the leaves as vapour, gathers into clouds above the canopy, and falls back as rain onto the same forest.
Follow a single droplet all the way around the loop (roots → leaf → vapour → cloud → rain → roots), stepping through one stage at a time.
Use a 'how many trees?' control to reduce the number of trees, and observe what happens to the vapour, the clouds, and the rain.
Add trees back and describe, in your own words, what happens to the clouds and rainfall.
State the rule you discovered in the model: more trees → more transpiration → more rain; fewer trees → less transpiration → less rain.
activities.title: Run and perturb the forest's rain loop

feedback: If a learner confuses transpiration with breathing out CO2: clarify that transpiration is water vapour leaving through tiny pores in the leaf, not the gas exchange of respiration.
If a learner thinks the clouds appear for no reason: point to the rising-vapour stage — the vapour cools higher up and condenses into cloud.
If a learner draws a straight line sea → cloud → rain: keep the sea arrow but redirect them to close the loop back to the roots, because much of the rain falls on the forest and is drawn up again.
Confirm correct use: 'Yes — transpiration is water leaving the leaf as vapour.'
activities.intendedInsight: The water cycle in a rainforest is a closed loop with named stages, and transpiration is the specific step where water leaves the plant through its leaves as vapour.
learnerActions: Study a circular diagram of the forest water cycle with directional arrows connecting roots → leaves → rising vapour → cloud → rain → back to roots.
Select the leaf and state what happens there, using the word 'transpiration' (water escapes from the leaf as vapour).
For each stage, say in one line what is happening (e.g. 'here the vapour cools and condenses into cloud').
Explain why the arrows form a closed loop rather than a straight line.
activities.title: Label the loop and name each stage

feedback: If the order is wrong, point back to the loop diagram and trace one droplet's journey.
If the learner picks 'all rain blows in from the sea', remind them the leaves release vapour that forms clouds here.
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidate the sequence, the term 'transpiration', and the self-rain idea so they can be recalled and explained.
learnerActions: Put the five stages of the loop in the correct order: roots absorb water; leaves transpire; vapour rises; vapour cools and condenses into cloud; rain falls back to the roots.
Complete: 'Water leaves the leaf as vapour by a process called ____.' (transpiration)
Choose and justify the better statement: (a) all the rainforest's rain blows in from the sea; (b) the forest makes much of its own rain through transpiration.
activities.title: Order the stages and use the key word
